The research step assembles a thousand-token summary. The enrichment step adds five hundred tokens of company profile. Tool call responses add another few hundred. By the time the workflow reaches the synthesis step, the input can exceed the limit without any single step being unreasonable.

The production approach is to treat context as a budget, not as a dump. Each node receives only what it needs to do its job. The scoring node does not need the full research transcript. It needs the structured summary. The email drafting node does not need the tool call logs from the research phase. You assemble a purpose-built prompt for each node, not a growing accumulation of everything that happened before.

Three patterns keep context under budget. First, selective state inclusion. When a node calls the LLM, it builds the prompt from specific state fields, not the entire state. Write a function that extracts the relevant fields and formats them. If you forward the entire state, you will eventually hit the limit and produce a silently truncated prompt with no error signal.

Second, rolling summarization. For workflows that accumulate content across many phases, add a summarizer node after each major phase. It takes the full output and produces a condensed version within a fixed token budget. Later nodes receive the summary. The full output remains in graph state for debugging but is excluded from subsequent prompts. The budget is explicit and enforced, not left to grow unchecked.

Third, relevance filtering before prompt assembly. Before building the final RAG prompt, score each retrieved chunk against the query and drop chunks below a threshold. The context window fills with the most relevant content rather than the first N chunks by default.

One research finding worth knowing. Models perform worse on information placed in the middle of long contexts than at the beginning or end. This is called the lost-in-the-middle effect. For prompts that must include long context, put the most critical information first or last. If you are assembling a large company profile, lead with the fields the model needs most for the task and trail with supplementary details.

In the interview, if long-running agents or context limits come up, name this framework. Context as a budget. Selective state inclusion per node. Rolling summarization across phases. Relevance filtering before assembly. Important content at the edges to mitigate lost-in-the-middle. That answer shows you have built agents that run long enough to hit the real constraints.

chapters.title: Cron Architecture for Agent Systems
chapters.script:
Not every agent workflow is triggered by a user request. Some run on a schedule. A nightly enrichment pass. A weekly refresh of data that drifts. A daily cleanup of checkpoint rows that accumulate. Understanding how to wire cron triggers into a LangGraph system is a practical skill the interviewer may probe if you describe any background-processing use case.

The pattern has three layers. The scheduler layer fires at a wall-clock interval. The trigger layer translates that firing into a POST request against a specific endpoint in your application. The worker layer receives that request, looks up the appropriate graph, and invokes it.

In a serverless environment like Cloudflare Workers, the scheduler is a cron trigger defined in the wrangler configuration. It fires the worker's scheduled handler. That handler does one thing: it sends a POST to the backend container at a well-known route, such as slash cron slash tick. The handler then exits. All actual logic lives in the Python backend, not in the worker.

The tick endpoint receives the request and dispatches the appropriate graph. For a research loop that runs every five minutes, the tick endpoint invokes the research loop graph with a stable thread ID. The graph resumes from its last checkpoint, processes one batch of papers, and writes its updated state back. The thread ID persists across all invocations, so the graph's state accumulates across runs without re-processing what it already handled.

One critical detail for production cron systems: sequential invocation. If the cron fires every five minutes and each tick takes four minutes, two ticks may overlap. The second tick starts while the first is still writing to the database. In a single-worker system with a conservatively sized connection pool, overlapping ticks share the same pool and can starve each other. The solution is a concurrency gate that prevents the second tick from starting until the first completes.

At the database level, Postgres advisory locks are the right tool. Before the tick starts, it tries to acquire an advisory lock keyed to the graph's slug. If the lock is already held by a running tick, the try-acquire returns false immediately. The new tick exits without doing any work. No waiting, no blocking. The lock holder completes its work and the lock releases automatically when the database session closes.

Session-scoped advisory locks are self-healing. If the backend process dies while holding a lock, Postgres releases the lock when the connection closes. There is no stuck lock. No manual cleanup. No separate TTL mechanism. The next tick that runs will acquire the lock cleanly and proceed.

The advisory lock handles ticks that are still actively running. There is a complementary pattern for detecting ticks that crashed after writing an in-progress row but before completing. At the start of each tick, before attempting to acquire the lock, the endpoint queries for rows that have been in the in-progress state longer than the cron interval — say, more than ten minutes old for a ten-minute cron. Those rows represent crashed processes. The current tick marks them as crashed, records the reason, and continues with its normal acquire-and-run cycle. The lock itself is already free because the crashed session closed when the process died. The two mechanisms together cover every failure mode: a running tick backs off cleanly, and a crashed tick is detected, marked, and swept on the next healthy firing.

Beyond the research loop, cron jobs serve as a maintenance layer for the whole system. A daily checkpoint pruning job truncates the LangGraph checkpoint tables to prevent unbounded database growth. Long-running systems with many threads accumulate checkpoint rows that are never read again. Without periodic pruning, the checkpoint tables grow until they exceed the storage budget. The pruning job runs at a quiet time of day and keeps the tables lean.

In the interview, if you describe any periodic or background processing in your system, name the cron architecture explicitly. Scheduler trigger, POST to tick endpoint, advisory lock gate, sequential invocation, checkpoint pruning. Those specifics show you have thought about the operational reality of background agents, not just the logic they run.

chapters.title: Distributed Coordination with Advisory Locks
chapters.script:
When multiple instances of a system can all attempt the same operation simultaneously, you need a coordination layer. The operation should happen exactly once, or at most once per time window. The coordination layer decides which instance proceeds and which ones back off.

The simplest coordination mechanism that fits agent systems is a Postgres advisory lock. Advisory locks are lightweight, transactional, and self-healing. They cost one database round trip to acquire and release. They do not create rows, do not affect table statistics, and do not require schema changes. They are ideal for coordinating short-lived operations between concurrent processes.

The try-acquire variant is non-blocking. It returns a boolean. True means the lock was acquired and this instance should proceed. False means another instance holds the lock and this instance should back off immediately. There is no timeout, no queue, no blocking. Each instance either wins the race and proceeds, or loses the race and exits cleanly.

The lock key is a bigint. Since most coordination is keyed on a string — a slug, a job name, a resource identifier — you convert the string to a bigint using a hash. Taking the first eight bytes of SHA-256 and interpreting them as a signed sixty-four-bit integer gives a stable, collision-resistant key. The probability of two different strings mapping to the same lock key is negligible for the small number of keys a production system uses.

The self-healing property matters for production reliability. A lock held by a session is released automatically when that session closes, whether the session closed gracefully or because the process was killed. There is no scenario where a crashed process leaves a permanently held lock. The next tick, the next container restart, the next invocation — all will find the lock available.

In the interview, if the conversation reaches distributed coordination, this is the practical answer for agent systems. You do not need Redis. You do not need ZooKeeper. If you already have a Postgres database, advisory locks give you process-level coordination with no additional infrastructure. Name the mechanism, describe the try-acquire pattern, mention the self-healing property, and explain how you derive the lock key from a string. That answer is specific and implementable.

chapters.title: Graceful Shutdown and Lifespan
chapters.script:
Agent systems run long-lived operations. A pipeline that fans out to five hundred companies and takes forty minutes to complete cannot be killed instantly without losing work. A container restart during active runs needs to preserve as much in-flight state as possible. Graceful shutdown is how you protect that work.

The ASGI lifespan protocol gives you two hooks. The startup hook runs before the application begins serving requests. The shutdown hook runs after the server stops accepting new requests but before the process exits. In an agent system, the startup hook compiles all the graphs, opens the database connection pool, and builds the remote adapter registry. The shutdown hook drains in-flight background tasks and closes all network connections.

The drain window is time-bounded. In production, twenty seconds is the default, configurable via an environment variable. The shutdown hook wraps the drain in asyncio.wait_for with that timeout. When the deadline passes, wait_for raises TimeoutError, which the handler catches. It then cancels every task that has not yet finished and gathers them a second time to let the cancellations propagate. That second gather matters: it gives each node's finally block a chance to run and release database connections before the pool itself shuts down. Without it, tasks get cancelled and the pool closes simultaneously, and the finally blocks raise errors into an already-closed pool.

There is a reference-management detail that trips people up. Python's event loop does not keep strong references to asyncio tasks. A fire-and-forget task created with asyncio.create_task can be garbage-collected before it finishes if nothing else holds a reference to it. To prevent silent mid-run GC, every background task gets added to a module-level set when it starts and removed when it completes. The shutdown hook iterates that set to collect every in-flight task before draining. Without the set, the drain finds nothing to wait for and the shutdown proceeds as if all runs completed cleanly, even if they were silently discarded.

Remote adapters need explicit teardown. Each adapter holds an HTTP connection pool to a remote container. If those connections are not closed cleanly at shutdown, the remote container may hold them open for several minutes waiting for data that will never arrive. Closing each adapter in the shutdown hook lets the remote connection pools recycle cleanly. The teardown wraps each close call in its own exception handler so a misbehaving remote cannot block the shutdown of all the others.

There is a startup-failure contract worth knowing. If the lifespan startup hook fails, the container should stay alive rather than exit. A crash on startup means the orchestration layer will restart the container immediately, which may crash again, which will restart again, creating a restart loop that prevents manual investigation. Keeping the container alive on startup failure means an engineer can exec into the running container, check the logs, and diagnose the problem without chasing a constantly restarting process.

A related contract applies when compilation is partial. In a system with seventy or more graphs, one graph may fail to compile — a missing environment variable, an import error in a dependency, an incompatible library version — while the rest compile cleanly. The correct behavior is to collect per-graph failures rather than raising on the first one. The container starts, serves the sixty-nine graphs that compiled successfully, and exposes the failure list at a health endpoint. The alternative, raising the first failure and aborting startup, causes the same crash loop problem and additionally makes all working graphs unavailable. An operator inspecting the health endpoint can see exactly which graph failed and why, redeploy just the fix, and restore full service without taking down anything that was already working.

In the interview, if you describe the operational lifecycle of a containerized agent system, name these three startup behaviors explicitly. Compile graphs at startup, not per request, so the first request does not pay the compilation cost. Drain in-flight background tasks at shutdown with a configurable time bound. Close remote adapters individually so one misbehaving remote does not block the others. Those three behaviors show you have thought about the container lifecycle, not just the graph logic inside it.

chapters.title: Evaluating Prompt and Model Changes
chapters.script:
When a hiring manager asks how you evaluate model quality, the wrong answer is to say you test it manually. The right answer is to describe a repeatable evaluation pipeline that catches regressions before they reach production.

The building block is an eval dataset. A set of input-output pairs that represent the range of cases your workflow handles. Good cases, edge cases, cases that broke in the past. The dataset grows over time, especially by capturing production failures: whenever the system produces a wrong answer that reaches users, that example goes into the eval set. It is now a regression test.

The evaluation pipeline runs that dataset against a candidate change — a prompt edit, a new model, a temperature adjustment — and scores the outputs. The scoring can be rule-based, model-based, or both. Rule-based scoring applies deterministic checks: does the output parse as valid JSON, does it contain the required fields, does the score field fall within the expected range. Model-based scoring asks a judge model to evaluate the output against a rubric: is this email professionally appropriate, does this summary accurately reflect the source document, is this ICP assessment consistent with the provided criteria.

LangSmith and Langfuse both have built-in eval runners. You provide the dataset and the scoring functions, and the platform runs the inputs through the candidate and scores the results. The output is a table of pass rate, mean score, and per-example diffs against the baseline. A prompt change that lifts the mean score by five percent while keeping pass rate stable is a candidate worth shipping. A model upgrade that improves average quality but introduces three new failure modes is not.

One pattern that scales well is the sandwich eval. You run the eval dataset against the current production prompt as the baseline, then against the candidate change, then diff the two. Any example where the candidate is worse than baseline is a regression. You review regressions manually before shipping. The candidate only ships if the regression count is zero or the regressions are in cases you judged acceptable.

In the interview, when evaluation comes up, name these pieces. Eval dataset built from edge cases and production failures. Scoring that combines deterministic checks with a judge model. Baseline-versus-candidate diffing. Regression review before shipping. That answer describes a real quality gate, not a vibe check.

chapters.title: Testing Agent Components
chapters.script:
A LangGraph workflow is software. Like any other software, you can test the pieces independently. Most teams that build agent systems skip this, which means bugs in routing logic, reducer behavior, and tool implementations surface only in production. A test suite for agent components catches these earlier and makes refactoring safer.

There are three layers to test: individual nodes, graph topology, and tool implementations.

Testing individual nodes is straightforward. A node is a function that takes a state dict and returns a dict of updates. You call it directly with a test state, capture the return value, and assert on the updates. The LLM call inside the node is the part you mock. Replace the LLM wrapper with a function that returns a canned response for the test input. The node logic — how it interprets the LLM response, what it writes to state, what checks it runs before calling the model — is fully testable without any API calls or token spend.

Testing graph topology means verifying that edges route correctly without running the full graph. LangGraph exposes the compiled graph's structure. You can assert that a specific node has the expected successors, that a conditional edge evaluates to the right next node for a given state, and that the terminal nodes are the ones you expect. These tests catch routing bugs where a refactor moved a node but forgot to update an edge.

Testing tool implementations is where you have the most leverage. Tools are regular functions. A tool that calls a database, an external API, or a file system is testable with a controlled or in-memory version of each dependency. If your research tool fetches a web page, inject a fake HTTP client that returns a fixture. If your scoring tool queries Postgres, run tests against a local instance. Tools are where most agent bugs actually live, and they are the easiest part of the system to test in isolation.

One test category specific to LangGraph: reducer behavior under parallel writes. Write a test that creates a state with a reducer-annotated field, simulates two concurrent updates to that field, and asserts that the reducer merged them rather than clobbering one. This is exactly the failure mode described in the reducer clobbering section of production failures, and it is easy to verify in a deterministic unit test before it becomes a production incident.

In the interview, if testing comes up, give these four categories. Node logic with mocked LLM responses. Topology assertions for routing and edges. Tool implementations with controlled dependencies. Reducer behavior under parallel writes. That answer treats agents as testable software rather than systems that can only be evaluated end-to-end through expensive live runs.

chapters.title: Questions to Ask the Interviewer
chapters.script:
At the end of every interview, they ask if you have questions. This is not a courtesy. It is a continuation of the evaluation. The questions you ask reveal how you think.

Here are eight questions worth asking. Each one signals something specific.

Ask about the team's current observability stack. You want to understand how they trace LLM calls today, whether they measure cost per run, and whether they have dashboards for latency. This signals that you think in operations, not just development.

Ask about the biggest reliability challenge they have faced in the last six months. This surfaces real problems. You learn something about where the system actually breaks and you demonstrate that you know production systems have real failure histories, not just theoretical ones.

Ask about how human review is integrated into automated workflows. This shows you understand that agents touch real systems and that the boundary between automation and oversight is a design decision worth asking about.

Ask about the cost model. How do they track LLM spend. Is it per user, per tenant, per feature. Are there budgets per run or per day. This demonstrates that you think about the commercial reality of shipping LLM features.

Ask about the on-call rotation. Who gets paged when an agent workflow degrades at three in the morning. This shows you understand that production AI systems create operational responsibilities, not just user-facing features.

Ask about the evaluation strategy for new models and prompt changes. How do they assess whether a model upgrade improved or degraded quality before shipping it. This signals that you think about quality as a measured property, not a subjective judgment.

Ask about the hardest thing to debug they have encountered. This is an invitation for a real story. People who have run LLM systems in production have stories. The best ones involve silent failures. Listening carefully and asking follow-up questions shows engagement and technical fluency.

Ask what the team uses to decide between building on top of a framework like LangGraph and building a custom orchestration layer. This is a sophisticated systems design question. It shows you know there are alternatives and you want to understand their architectural philosophy.

You will not have time for all eight. Pick three. The best three for this role are usually observability, reliability, and evaluation strategy. Those three span the whole product development lifecycle. They tell the interviewer that you think from shipping to monitoring to improving, not just from prototyping to launch.

chapters.title: Supervisor Graphs and Partial Failure
chapters.script:
A supervisor graph runs other graphs as subgraphs. It sequences them, catches their errors, and continues with whatever succeeded. This pattern matters more than it sounds. In a system that runs four or five analytical passes over a company before drafting an outreach email, you cannot afford to lose the entire run because one pass times out.

Here is the contract. Each subgraph node is wrapped in a try-except. If the subgraph raises, the exception message is written to a state field called subgraph errors, under a key that identifies which subgraph failed. The graph does not abort. It continues to the next subgraph. When all subgraphs have run, a final synthesizer node reads the subgraph errors field and knows which passes completed and which did not.

The synthesizer does two things with that information. First, it builds a human-readable partial failure note. If the pricing subgraph failed and the competitive analysis subgraph succeeded, the note says pricing data is unavailable for this run. Second, it passes that note into the LLM prompt for the synthesis step. The model is explicitly told what data is missing. It responds with a synthesis that acknowledges the gaps rather than inventing data to fill them.

There is a design subtlety in the error accumulation. Multiple subgraphs run in sequence, each potentially writing to subgraph errors. The reducer for that field uses last-write-wins for each key individually, which is safe because each subgraph writes under its own unique key. There is no collision. The final subgraph errors dict contains one entry per failed subgraph, with the truncated exception message as the value.

The graph stamps the partial failures list into the graph meta field before completing, so the caller can inspect it without parsing the internals of the state. An API consumer polling the run result sees a top-level partial failures array. Each entry has the subgraph name and the reason. The run is marked complete, not errored. It produced a result. It just produced a partial one.

In the interview, the vocabulary to use is: supervisor graph, subgraph errors, partial failure contract, synthesizer with gap acknowledgment. The key insight to communicate is that partial completion is a first-class outcome in a well-designed system. The alternative, aborting the whole run on any single subgraph failure, is cheaper to implement and much worse for users. A supervisor that produces a partial result with a clear explanation is more valuable than one that produces nothing.

The same partial-failure thinking applies at the stage level. A multi-stage pipeline needs a status vocabulary that distinguishes four outcomes, not two. A stage that processed inputs and produced results with no errors is OK. A stage that produced some results despite encountering errors is PARTIAL — useful output came out, but not all of it. A stage that encountered errors and produced nothing is FAIL. A stage that was never attempted because its input queue was empty is SKIP. These four states are mutually exclusive and complete. A caller that reads them can decide whether to continue, flag the run for review, or halt immediately. The insight is that PARTIAL and SKIP are not degraded forms of FAIL. A partial result tells the operator which records succeeded and which did not. A skipped stage tells them nothing was attempted — possibly because an earlier stage filtered everything out. Collapsing these four into binary pass-fail produces a less informative run report and makes diagnosis slower.

chapters.title: Prompt Engineering at Scale
chapters.script:
Prompt engineering in production is not about craft. It is about contracts.

A prompt in production is a contract between the caller and the model. The caller promises to provide specific fields in a specific format. The model promises to return a specific JSON shape. Both sides of the contract need to be stable across model upgrades, parameter changes, and context variations. That stability requires discipline.

Three practices make prompts stable at scale. First, always specify the output format in the system prompt, not the user turn. The system prompt defines the model's role and the output contract. The user turn provides the variable input. If you put the JSON output instruction in the user turn, it competes with the user content for the model's attention and is more likely to be ignored under pressure. Put it in the system prompt and it is part of the model's identity for the duration of the call.

Second, separate drafting temperature from refinement temperature. A drafting step benefits from some variability. You want the model to generate something interesting, not the statistically most probable output. A temperature around zero point five works well. A refinement step is editing, not generating. You want the model to make small, deliberate changes to an existing draft. A temperature around zero point two reduces the chance of the model rewriting the whole thing when you only wanted it to tighten one paragraph.

Third, use mode-switching prompts rather than conditional logic in prompts. If a feature has two distinct use cases with different goals, write two separate system prompts and select between them at the call site. A single prompt with conditional branches and nested instructions becomes harder to maintain, harder to test, and harder to explain to the model. Two clean prompts with clear roles are easier to debug and easier to version independently.

A concrete example: the email drafting graph serves two personas. One is an engineer applying for roles, replying to LinkedIn messages and contact-page submissions. The other is a sales operator sending outbound to GitHub-sourced leads. The tone objectives, sender backstories, and appropriate constraints are completely different. Rather than a single prompt with nested persona blocks and conditional language, the graph selects between two system prompts at call time based on a sender_mode parameter. The output format specification, length constraints, and prohibited phrase list stay in a shared prefix that both prompts inherit. Only the identity block switches. The two prompts are versioned, tested, and evolved independently. A regression in the sales persona cannot bleed into the job-seek persona because they are separate strings with separate eval datasets.

One more practice that scales. Never let the output schema live only in the prompt. Define it as a TypedDict or Pydantic model in code. Parse the model's JSON output against that schema immediately after the call. If the parse fails, that is a structured error you can retry with the schema as explicit feedback in the next attempt. If the parse succeeds, you have a typed object downstream, not a raw dict that might be missing fields.

The concrete form of that feedback matters more than the principle. When Pydantic raises a validation error, it produces a structured list of error objects, each carrying the field path, the violation type, and the offending value. Serialize that list as JSON and inject it into the user message for the next attempt alongside an explicit instruction to correct the structure. The same pattern applies to any domain constraint you detect post-parse: a subject line that exceeds fifty characters, a banned phrase in the body, a score outside the expected range. Detect the violation with your own code, name the specific phrase or value that failed, and inject that as a named constraint into the next attempt's user turn. The model receives exactly what it got wrong and what the corrected form must satisfy. A two-attempt loop with structured violation feedback typically resolves the problem on the second try without needing a broader retry budget or a prompt rewrite.

In the interview, when asked about prompt engineering best practices, give these four. Output format in the system prompt. Separate temperatures for drafting and refinement. Mode-switching prompts over conditional mega-prompts. Output schema defined in code and parsed immediately. Those four practices demonstrate that you have shipped prompts in production and dealt with their failure modes.

chapters.title: Mock Interview: Full Walkthrough
chapters.script:
Let me walk you through a strong thirty-minute technical screen. The interviewer opens with a system design question, drills on a specific mechanism, introduces a debugging scenario, and closes with a pressure question. Watch how each transition works.

The interviewer opens. Tell me about a system you have built that involved multiple LLM calls working together. The candidate answers. I built a pipeline that takes a list of target companies and enriches each one. For each company, the pipeline runs four parallel steps: deep ICP research, competitor analysis, pricing analysis, and go-to-market assessment. Each step is a separate LangGraph subgraph. They run in sequence under a supervisor graph. If one fails, the supervisor records the failure and continues with the others. The final step synthesizes all the successful outputs into a product intelligence report.

That answer gave the interviewer four things to drill on: the parallelism claim, the supervisor pattern, the failure handling, and the synthesizer. The interviewer picks the one that distinguishes senior candidates. They pick failure handling.

The interviewer drills. What happens to the state when one of those subgraphs fails mid-run and the exception propagates. The candidate does not pause. Each node in the supervisor is wrapped in a try-except. If the pricing subgraph raises, the exception message gets written to a field called subgraph errors, under the key run-pricing. The graph does not abort. It continues to the next subgraph. At the end, the synthesizer reads subgraph errors, builds a note that says pricing data is unavailable, and passes it into the synthesis prompt so the model acknowledges the gap rather than hallucinating pricing data.

The interviewer nods. That answer showed the specific mechanism, not just the concept. Now they switch to debugging.

The interviewer changes direction. A user says the product intelligence report for one company has completely wrong competitor information. You have traces. Walk me through the debug. The candidate starts correctly. First I open the trace and find the competitor analysis subgraph for that specific run. I look at the span for the LLM call that produced the competitor list. I check the input. Did the retrieved competitor data match the actual company, or did the retrieval return documents from a different industry.

The interviewer pushes. The trace shows a successful call with the right company name in the prompt. What now. The candidate does not freeze. If the prompt looks correct and the model still produced wrong competitors, I look at the retrieved context in detail. The model may have received a document from a competitor's competitor, not the target company's competitor. Embedding similarity is not the same as factual relevance. A document about a company in the same space can score high on embedding similarity while being about a different segment. I would check the reranker score if there is one, and look at whether a metadata filter was supposed to constrain retrieval and was bypassed.

That answer names the mechanism, proposes a specific hypothesis, and shows the next investigative step. The interviewer marks it as strong.

The pressure question comes at the end. The interviewer asks something the candidate has not seen. You are designing the checkpointing strategy for this system. The enrichment phase takes forty minutes across five hundred companies. How do you decide which threads need resumable checkpoints and which do not. The candidate uses the composure pattern. I have not designed that exact decision framework before, but here is how I would think about it. The question is whether the run produces intermediate state that is expensive to reconstruct. A single-company enrichment worker runs in two minutes. If it dies, you restart it. Not worth a resumable checkpoint. But the coordinator that dispatches all five hundred workers and collects results is running for forty minutes. If that container restarts at minute thirty-five, losing five hundred companies of accumulated results is expensive. That thread gets a resumable checkpoint with a stable thread ID that survives restarts.

The interviewer closes the conversation. That final answer demonstrates cost-benefit reasoning applied to a specific architectural decision. That is the kind of thinking the hiring manager wants to hire.

chapters.title: Prompt Templates as Contracts
chapters.script:
Let me go one level deeper on the prompt engineering practices, because the most common failure mode in production LLM features is not a bad prompt. It is a fragile prompt.

A fragile prompt breaks when the input changes. It was written for one specific input format and tested with one specific example. In production, input comes from ten different callers, each with slightly different formatting. The model receives a malformed template, produces garbage, and the downstream parse fails silently.

The defense is to treat the prompt template as part of the data model. Every variable that gets interpolated into the prompt should have a type. Every optional section should have a fallback. The template should be testable independently of the model, with a function that takes the input dict and returns the assembled prompt string. If that function raises on bad input, you catch it before the model call.

Here is a pattern that works in production. Write the prompt template as a Python function, not a string. The function takes typed arguments and returns a list of messages in the format the model expects. If a required field is missing, the function raises a ValueError with a clear message. If an optional field is absent, the function uses a sensible default, documented in the code. The function is unit-testable without touching the API. You can verify that the prompt assembles correctly for edge-case inputs without spending tokens.

The same principle applies to the output schema. Define the expected output as a Python TypedDict or Pydantic model before you write the prompt. Then write the prompt's output specification based on that model. If the schema changes, the prompt description and the parsing code change together. They cannot drift apart because they reference the same source of truth.

Temperature settings belong in the function signature, not buried in a configuration file. When a developer reads the call to make an LLM, they should see the temperature directly. They should understand why it was set to that value. A drafting temperature of zero point five and a refinement temperature of zero point two communicate their intent. A temperature read from an env var called LLM TEMP communicates nothing.

In the interview, if prompt engineering comes up, these are the three production practices that matter: prompts as typed functions with validated inputs, output schemas defined in code and parsed immediately, and temperatures as explicit parameters with documented intent. Those three practices apply equally whether you are using OpenAI, Anthropic, or an open-weight model.

chapters.title: Specialized Models for Specialized Tasks
chapters.script:
There is a design decision that separates intermediate engineers from senior ones. It is knowing when to call a general-purpose LLM and when to call something smaller and more specialized instead.

Here is the pattern in the lead-gen system. The pipeline needs to assign every contact a priority tier. Not a free-form label. A structured score from A down to D, with reasons, that the outreach queue uses to decide who to contact first. The naive approach is to send the contact's profile to the same general-purpose LLM that writes the emails. Feed it a long prompt describing the scoring criteria. Ask it to return tier plus reasons.

The problem with that approach is variability. A general LLM produces valid but inconsistent output depending on what else is in the prompt, what temperature you are using, and what the model saw during training. For a scoring task with a known output schema and a small fixed vocabulary, variability is a defect, not a feature.

The production solution is a LoRA fine-tuned on a small model. In this case, Qwen2.5-1.5B, quantized to four-bit precision and served from a single-node inference endpoint. The model was fine-tuned on labeled contact profiles and produces the tier, the score, and up to five reasons directly. The graph that calls it is a single node. Profile text goes in. Structured JSON comes out.

The engineering challenge is the cold-start problem. The inference endpoint runs on a free-tier environment. After a period of idle, it shuts down. The first request after that idle period has to wait thirty to sixty seconds for the container to restart before it can respond. Warm calls return in a few seconds. Cold calls can take nearly a minute.

The graph handles this with a generous timeout. Ninety seconds. That sounds unreasonable until you compare it to the alternative, which is a timeout error on the first request and a failed tier assignment. The caller knows the endpoint may be cold and budgets for it. The trade-off is explicit: we accept occasional long latency on the first call in exchange for not running inference infrastructure ourselves.

The profile that gets sent to the model is not the raw database record. It is serialized into a structured text format. Each field gets its own labeled line: name, title, company. Then company size, LinkedIn headline, bio. Then skills, experience level, seniority, department. Each field is prefixed with a key in all caps — NAME, TITLE, COMPANY — so the model always knows what it is reading. The format is consistent across every call, which is what lets the fine-tuned model generalize. A LoRA trained on inconsistent input formats is a LoRA that scores inconsistently.

If the endpoint returns a tier value outside the expected set, the graph substitutes D rather than propagating a bad value. If the score field cannot be parsed as a float, it defaults to zero. The downstream caller always gets a valid structured response. The fallback logic is in the graph node, not in every call site that uses the graph.

In the interview, this pattern answers a question you will get in some form: how do you decide when to use an LLM versus a more specialized approach. The answer is: general-purpose LLMs are the right tool when the task requires flexible language understanding and when variability in style is acceptable. Specialized fine-tuned models are the right tool when the output schema is fixed, the task is narrow, and consistency matters more than flexibility. For scoring, classifying, or labeling at high volume, the specialized model wins.

chapters.title: Scoring Fit Without an LLM
chapters.script:
There is another layer below the fine-tuned model. For company-level fit, the production system uses classical machine learning. A logistic regression over a set of numeric features. No LLM involved at all.

The reason is computational. The pipeline processes companies at scale. Each company needs a fit score. Running an LLM call per company would be slow and expensive. Running a logistic regression over a feature vector takes microseconds. NumPy handles batching, and you get scores for hundreds of companies in the time a single LLM call would take.

The feature weights are explicit and tunable. Industry match gets twenty-five points. Seniority match also gets twenty-five points. Employee count in range gets fifteen. Department match gets fifteen. Tech stack overlap gets ten. Email presence gets five. These weights are not hardcoded. They live in a configuration file that the operations team can adjust as the ideal customer profile evolves without redeploying code.

At the company level, the features are different but the approach is the same. The model asks whether the company has an AI tier score, whether it has a GitHub presence with an AI signal, whether it appears on Hugging Face, what its stated intent score is, whether it has decision-maker contacts already in the database. Each of these is a numeric feature. The logistic regression maps the feature vector to a probability. The probability gets calibrated with isotonic regression using pool-adjacent-violators, which is the standard technique for ensuring that a probability of sixty percent actually corresponds to sixty percent of positive cases in the training data.

The output is a calibrated probability, not a raw score. That distinction matters in production. A raw logistic score can drift outside sensible bounds when input features are out-of-distribution. A calibrated probability stays interpretable. When the score says seventy percent, you can trust that it means something close to what you think it means.

The reason to know this for the interview is not because the interviewer will quiz you on pool-adjacent-violators. It is because the underlying question is always the same: where is the intelligence in this system, and how does it stay reliable. A system that delegates all decisions to a general-purpose LLM is a system where the intelligence is opaque and the failure modes are unpredictable. A system that reserves LLMs for tasks that need flexible language generation and uses calibrated classical models for classification and scoring is a system where the intelligence is visible, auditable, and tunable.

Know the difference and say it clearly. That distinction lands every time.

One more scoring pattern worth having ready: weighted composite scoring when multiple dimensions matter and no single dimension should dominate. The research pipeline selects a champion paper to synthesize using exactly this approach. Each candidate receives a composite score built from three factors. Novelty carries forty percent of the weight — it captures how much unexplored territory exists around the paper's contribution. Research cluster size carries thirty percent, normalized against a ceiling of a hundred members so that an enormous cluster does not swamp the other signals. Reviewer availability carries the remaining thirty percent, normalized against twenty suggested contacts. The three terms sum to a composite between zero and one. Ties resolve in two further steps: a separate quality score from a two-pass evaluation, then paper age with the earliest paper winning.

The normalization step is the key design decision. Without it, a dimension with a wide natural range swamps everything else regardless of its assigned weight. A member count of five hundred would dominate a novelty score of zero point nine even if novelty is supposed to carry forty percent of the decision. Normalizing each dimension to a zero-to-one range before applying weights makes the weights mean what they say. Name this pattern in the interview — weights, normalization ceilings, tiebreaker chain — and you show you have built ranking systems past the point where the naive version breaks.

chapters.title: Deterministic Prompt Variation
chapters.script:
When you run a research pipeline that scores hundreds of paper gap analyses, you will eventually want to know whether one prompting strategy outperforms another. The naive approach is random selection — flip a coin per call and pick variant A or B. Random selection creates a debugging problem. If the pipeline retries a failed call, the retry may receive a different variant than the original. If you want to replay a specific case to understand why it scored the way it did, you cannot reproduce the exact prompt without having logged which variant was selected. A/B analysis becomes contaminated by retry collisions, and any conclusion about which variant is better is confounded by which calls happened to be retried.

The production fix is hash-based selection. Take the first eight characters of the gap signature — a stable identifier for the research gap being analyzed — parse them as a hexadecimal integer, and take the result modulo the number of variants. The same gap gets the same variant on every call, independent of retries, reruns, or timing. In the lead-gen system this gives four variants — baseline, critique-forward, applications-forward, and theory-forward — and any gap's assignment is deterministic and inspectable without storing it explicitly.

The same hash-based selection works for any parameter you want to vary without randomness: prompt tone, output format, model tier. The principle is that if reproducibility and debuggability matter, replace the coin flip with a hash of a stable identifier. The selection becomes part of the input's identity rather than an external random draw.

In the interview, if A/B testing or prompt variation comes up, name this constraint. Randomness in prompt selection is convenient but breaks reproducibility. Hash-based selection costs nothing and preserves both.

chapters.title: Fan-Out Deduplication
chapters.script:
A contact discovery graph fans out across multiple sources — GitHub profiles, academic databases, professional networks — and merges the results into a single candidate list. When two sources return the same person, the naive merge produces duplicate records. Downstream, that means double outreach, which burns the contact's goodwill and signals low quality to email providers.

Deduplication for this problem runs in two stages, and the distinction between stages matters. The first pass is in-memory, during the fan-out merge itself. While consolidating results from multiple sources, records are grouped by full name — first name and last name, both lowercased. When two records map to the same key, the merge combines their source lists, raises the confidence score by ten percentage points up to a cap of ninety-five percent, and unions their tag sets. A researcher found in both GitHub and an academic database emerges from the merge with both source attributions, elevated confidence, and the union of whatever tags each source assigned.

The second pass is against the database. After the in-memory merge, any record whose email guess or GitHub handle already appears in the contacts table is filtered out. This removes duplicates against prior pipeline runs, not just duplicates within the current batch.

Keeping these two passes separate is a deliberate design choice. The in-memory pass handles cross-source duplicates in the current batch without any database round-trips. The DB pass handles historical duplicates using a targeted lookup against only the surviving merged candidates. Collapsing both into a single database query would require a full contacts scan per record as the table grows. The two-stage structure keeps each pass fast and the logic for each duplicate type legible on its own.

chapters.title: Concurrent Cursor Partitioning
chapters.script:
A background research loop runs multiple seed queries simultaneously. Each query independently pages through a remote API — one might be on page three of an OpenAlex result set while another is exhausted and a third is still at the beginning of its Arxiv results. Storing all of that pagination state in a single shared cursor field creates a write collision. If two queries complete around the same time and both try to write back their updated cursor position, one write will overwrite the other. The pipeline silently loses a cursor position and cannot recover it without replaying from the beginning.

The production solution partitions the cursor state by query index inside a JSONB column. Each seed query writes back only its own key, using PostgreSQL's JSONB merge operator — double pipe characters — which patches the specified key without touching any other entries in the column. If query zero and query five finish concurrently and both write their cursor updates, the database applies both independently. Neither write interferes with the other. Each of the eight seed queries can be in a completely different state — different page depth, different exhaustion flag, different results-per-page count — without any coordination between them.

This is the general pattern for concurrent state in a shared row. Identify what unit of work each writer exclusively owns. Key each writer's state under a stable identifier. Patch only that key using a merge operator rather than a full column replacement. The writers can proceed in any order without coordination.

In the interview, if background processing or concurrent state comes up, describe this as JSONB key-scoped writes. It is the alternative to either a pessimistic row lock, which serializes all writes, or a full row update, which clobbers concurrent changes. JSONB merge lets concurrent writers coexist on the same row without coordination overhead.

chapters.title: Lazy Semaphore Initialization
chapters.script:
When you build a contact enrichment graph that calls multiple external APIs simultaneously, you need to cap concurrent requests per source. The natural tool is an asyncio semaphore — create one per source with a concurrency limit derived from the API's rate budget, and every outbound call acquires the semaphore before proceeding and releases it after.

The tricky part is where you initialize those semaphores. If you create them at module import time, you bind them to whatever event loop was running at import time. LangGraph spawns graph runs under different event loops. When a run tries to acquire a semaphore created in a prior loop, Python raises a RuntimeError about running under the wrong event loop. The fix is to defer initialization until the first use: check if the global variable is None, and if so, create the semaphore inside the running async context. That way the semaphore is always bound to the loop that will actually use it.

The concurrency limits are not arbitrary. They are derived from each API's published rate budget divided by the expected calls per contact. GitHub allows five thousand authenticated requests per hour. Each contact enrichment needs roughly twelve GitHub calls. That gives you a safe limit of eight concurrent contact enrichments — any more and you risk hitting the hourly cap during a burst. ORCID's public rate limit is twenty-four requests per second, which maps to four concurrent workers. Semantic Scholar allows one request per second with an API key, which maps to two. These are explicit engineering decisions, not tuning guesses. When an API changes its rate limits, you update the semaphore ceiling and the comment that explains why it is set where it is.

In the interview, if concurrency in an agent workflow comes up, name this pattern: per-source asyncio semaphores, lazily initialized to avoid event-loop binding errors, with ceilings derived from API rate budgets. That answer shows you have shipped concurrent enrichment pipelines and thought through the operational constraints of each external dependency.

chapters.title: PostgreSQL Advisory Locks
chapters.script:
There is a distributed exclusion pattern that requires no external service. No Redis. No Zookeeper. Just PostgreSQL, which you already have.

PostgreSQL advisory locks are session-scoped. Acquiring one marks that session as the exclusive holder of a specific integer key. Any other session that tries to acquire the same key will get false from pg_try_advisory_lock rather than waiting. When the session disconnects — whether by normal close or by a crash — the lock is automatically released. There is no TTL to set, no heartbeat to send, no cleanup job to run. The database handles the release.

The key is a signed 64-bit integer. To turn a human-readable identifier like a research slug into a stable lock key, you hash the slug with SHA-256, take the first eight bytes of the digest, and reinterpret them as a signed 64-bit big-endian integer. The same slug always produces the same key. The lock is deterministic and inspectable: you can query PostgreSQL's pg_locks table to see which slugs are currently held and which sessions hold them.

The pattern in the cron dispatch layer uses this to prevent two concurrent tick events from starting the same research loop. The tick handler hashes the seed slug, attempts pg_try_advisory_lock, and if it gets false, returns immediately. If it gets true, it runs the loop graph with a hard asyncio timeout and releases the lock in the finally block. The hard timeout ensures the lock is never held past the expected run duration. The explicit release in the finally block is belt-and-suspenders — the session close would release it anyway, but the explicit release is good practice and signals intent.

In the interview, when distributed coordination comes up, describe this as PostgreSQL session-advisory locks with slug-to-key derivation via SHA-256. The production advantage over Redis-based locks is that you have no additional service to operate, and the session-scoped auto-release property eliminates the entire class of stuck-lock incidents.

chapters.title: Batch Scoring with Cache Probing
chapters.script:
When you score contacts in a pipeline, you face a cost tradeoff. Calling the LLM once per contact is simple and robust but expensive — each call pays full input token cost. Batching multiple contacts into a single call with a shared system prompt is cheaper because the first call writes the system prompt into the cache and subsequent calls in the same batch read it at one-tenth the cost. The engineering question is how to handle partial failures without losing the cost benefit.

The production pattern is a two-level retry: batch first, per-item fallback. The node chunks the contact list into groups of eight. For each chunk, it assembles a single LLM call with the shared system prompt and all eight contact profiles in the user turn. On success, it parses the response and maps scores back to contact IDs. If the batch response is missing some indices — the model skipped a few contacts in its output — the node retries only the missing ones individually. The partial failure does not cascade into a full retry. The telemetry from the per-item retries folds back into the batch totals so cost accounting stays whole.

The cache effectiveness probe is the part most engineers miss. The first chunk in a batch run writes the system prompt to the cache. Every subsequent chunk should read it. After each chunk call, inspect the token usage response: if cache_read_input_tokens is zero on the second chunk and beyond, the prefix is not matching. Log a warning. The system prompt may have changed between chunks in a way you did not intend — an interpolated timestamp, a session ID in the prompt, a conditional branch that renders differently. The probe makes a cache miss visible rather than silently paying full price on every chunk.

In the interview, if batch LLM calls or prompt caching come up, give this pattern. Chunk into fixed-size batches. Retry missing indices per-item on failure. Verify cache effectiveness by checking cache_read_input_tokens on every chunk after the first. These three behaviors together give you the cost benefit of batching without sacrificing reliability or observability.

chapters.title: Circuit Breaker with Half-Open Probing
chapters.script:
A circuit breaker opens after a run of consecutive failures and stays open for a cool-down period. Every developer who has heard of circuit breakers knows this much. The part that separates production implementations from textbook ones is the half-open state.

When a circuit breaker has been open long enough, the next call is allowed through as a probe. If that probe succeeds, the circuit closes. If it fails, the cool-down resets. A naive implementation grants the probe a normal retry budget — the same number of attempts as any other call. This is wrong. A probe that fails is almost certain to fail repeatedly, and giving it three retries means every probe burns three round-trip timeouts before concluding the remote is still down. The production fix is to probe with a reduced budget of one. One attempt, no retries. If the remote responds successfully, the circuit closes. If not, the breaker resets the cool-down and waits again. The reduced probe budget prevents a still-broken remote from consuming full retry budgets on every probe attempt during the recovery window.

A related refinement applies when a remote service returns a 429 or 503 with a Retry-After header. Honoring that header is the baseline behavior. The jitter on top of it is the production insight. Without jitter, every parallel adapter in the system that hit the same rate limit will all retry at exactly the same moment the Retry-After window expires. They produce another burst, trigger another rate limit, and get another synchronized Retry-After. The fix is to add a small random offset — a few hundred milliseconds — so parallel adapters spread their retries across time rather than all firing at once.

In the interview, name the three behaviors of a production circuit breaker: normal-budget calls when closed, single-budget probes in half-open, and Retry-After with jitter to desynchronize parallel adapters. Those three details show you have shipped circuit breakers in a multi-instance environment, not just read about them.

chapters.title: The Retry Decision Tree
chapters.script:
When an outbound HTTP call returns a non-success status code, the question is whether to retry. Most teams apply one of two rules: retry on any failure, or retry only on network errors. Both rules fail in production.

Retry on any failure wastes budget on 4xx client errors that will never resolve. A 404 from a search API means the record does not exist. Retrying it three times changes nothing except latency and cost. Retry only on network errors misses the cases that most need retrying: 429 rate limit responses and 503 service unavailable responses, which are transient by definition.

The production decision tree has five branches. A 2xx or 3xx means success — stop. A 429 means the server is asking you to back off — honor the Retry-After if present, then retry. A 5xx is a judgment call per source: some APIs return 5xx for genuinely transient conditions, others return 5xx for permanent client errors like malformed queries. A 4xx that is not a 429 is a client error — fail fast, do not retry. A network error with no HTTP response means the connection was dropped — retry with backoff.

The per-source preset is the mechanism for encoding that judgment. Semantic Scholar returns 5xx codes for certain error conditions that will not resolve on retry, so its preset turns off 5xx retries. Arxiv returns 5xx for transient load issues, so its preset enables them. The decision tree stays the same. The configuration changes per source. When a new API is integrated, you look up its documentation, determine its 5xx semantics, and set the preset accordingly.

In the interview, give the five-branch decision tree by heart. It is short and precise, and it shows you have thought through the failure modes of external API calls rather than applying a blanket retry policy.

chapters.title: Async Generator Cleanup
chapters.script:
Long-running agent nodes stream their output through async generators. A research node that calls a remote graph might stream results for two hundred seconds. The generator holds an open HTTP connection to the remote service for the duration of that stream.

When the parent task is cancelled — because a timeout fired, because the supervisor graph decided to abort the run, because the user closed their session — Python cancels the coroutine. If the stream loop exits without explicitly closing the generator, the underlying HTTP connection stays open. The connection pool sees it as in use. A containerized backend with a pool of twenty connections can exhaust that pool in a few minutes of cancelled requests, causing all subsequent outbound calls to queue behind stale connections that will never be released.

The fix is a finally block that calls aclose on the generator. Open the generator, wrap the consumption loop in try, put the aclose call in finally. The finally block runs whether the loop exits normally, via exception, or via cancellation. To prevent the aclose call itself from masking a more important exception, wrap the aclose in its own try-except that logs and swallows any error from the cleanup. The rule is that finally blocks never raise. A broken aclose should not prevent the original cancellation signal from propagating.

In the interview, if streaming from remote services comes up, name this as async generator leak prevention: explicit aclose in a try-finally, with exception-tolerant cleanup. The connection pool exhaustion failure mode is concrete enough to show you have encountered this in production rather than reasoned about it from first principles.

chapters.title: Thread Delegation for Best-Effort Side Effects
chapters.script:
Not every database write in an agent system is on the critical path. Telemetry records, application logs, and audit traces are valuable but not worth crashing a graph run if they fail. The design principle is to treat these as best-effort side effects: fire them off, catch any error, log it, and continue regardless.

In an async codebase, the complication is that some of these writes use blocking database drivers — full synchronous connections rather than async pool checkouts. Running a blocking call on the async event loop stalls every other coroutine until it completes. During container cold-start, that stall can delay the readiness probe long enough to trigger a restart loop.

The fix is asyncio.to_thread. Wrap the synchronous database function and pass it to asyncio.to_thread — this delegates it to a thread pool worker and returns control to the event loop immediately. The calling node awaits the thread result, catches any database error, logs it, and proceeds. The node does not re-raise. A persistence failure is not a reason to abort a run that has already produced useful output.

This is a distinct pattern from converting the call to an async driver. If the write is genuinely best-effort — telemetry, logging, an audit upsert — converting it to async adds complexity without changing the failure semantics. Thread delegation with a swallowing try-except is the simpler and more honest design. The caller's intent is explicit: I want this to run without blocking, and I do not care if it fails.

In the interview, if non-critical I/O in async systems comes up, name this as thread delegation for best-effort writes. The insight is knowing which writes are on the critical path and which are not, and designing the error handling accordingly.

chapters.title: Per-Request Configuration in Middleware
chapters.script:
A small but production-important detail in middleware design: read configuration from environment variables inside the dispatch method, not at class construction time.

When configuration is read at construction, it is captured once and frozen. A test that patches an environment variable after the middleware class is instantiated sees the old value. Test isolation breaks when tests run in sequence and each test expects to control its own configuration state.

When configuration is read per-request — inside the dispatch method before applying any logic — the middleware reflects the current environment on every call. A test that sets an auth token before calling an endpoint works correctly. A test that removes the token to verify unauthenticated behavior works correctly. The middleware is stateless with respect to configuration.

The same principle applies to feature flags, rate limit thresholds, or any setting that changes across deployments or test scenarios. Reading at call time costs one dictionary lookup per request. The benefit is that the middleware becomes independently testable without requiring a full application rebuild between test cases.

A middleware factory makes this pattern compositional. Rather than a module-level singleton middleware class, the factory is a function that takes the configuration parameters — the env var name, the set of public paths that bypass auth — and returns a fresh class with those values closed over. Multiple apps in the same process can each call the factory with different parameters and get independent middleware with no shared mutable state between them.

In the interview, if request lifecycle or middleware design comes up, name this distinction: construction-time configuration is fast but inflexible, per-request configuration is trivially testable. For most middleware settings, the one-lookup overhead per request is negligible and the testing benefit is real.

chapters.title: Fan-Out with Sequential Pre-Stages
chapters.script:
When you design a contact enrichment graph, most data sources can run in parallel — ORCID, Semantic Scholar, PDF extraction, homepage scraping, LinkedIn. Each is independent. You fan out from a synthesis node, all six branches run concurrently, and you collect results at a join gate.

But some branches have internal dependencies. Enriching a GitHub profile requires a GitHub handle first. Without the handle, the profile fetch has nothing to call. You cannot fan out both steps from the same starting point because the second step depends on the output of the first.

The pattern is a sequential chain as a pre-stage within a branch. The GitHub branch runs two nodes in sequence: handle resolution, then profile enrichment. The handle resolution step starts in parallel with the other five branches. When it completes, it writes the resolved handle to state. The profile enrichment step picks up that handle and proceeds. Other branches are not blocked — they run fully independently. Only the GitHub profile enrichment waits on the handle resolution step, and only within its own branch.

The join gate is where all branches converge. In LangGraph, a node with multiple incoming edges acts as an implicit synchronization barrier. You draw one edge from each branch terminator to the convergence node. The graph waits for all predecessors before running it. No explicit gather, no asyncio.wait. The topology is the coordination mechanism.

Exception isolation completes the picture. Branches have different failure rates and different latencies. Semantic Scholar might be slow. PDF extraction might fail. Each branch catches its own exceptions internally and writes what it can to state. The convergence node receives whatever each branch produced and knows which sources completed and which did not. One slow branch delays the join but does not propagate its failure. One failed branch produces no result but does not cancel the others.

In the interview, name these three elements together: sequential pre-stages for intra-branch dependencies, implicit join gate via multiple incoming edges, and per-branch exception isolation for SLA diversity. The combination is what makes a fan-out graph robust rather than fragile.

chapters.title: Background Task Safety
chapters.script:
Two production hazards arise when you fire LLM tasks into the background without ceremony. The first is silent garbage collection. CPython's asyncio creates task objects with weak references by default. In a high-throughput environment, the garbage collector can collect a task object mid-execution if no strong reference holds it alive. The task appears to start, then silently disappears without completing or raising. This was a real Python behavior change in 3.11, and it is the reason every production-grade fire-and-forget implementation needs a strong reference strategy.

The fix is a module-level set. When you create a background task, add it to the set immediately after creation. Register a done callback that discards it from the set when the task finishes. The set holds a strong reference for the task's entire lifetime. The done callback ensures the set does not grow unbounded — completed tasks are removed automatically. A single module-level set protects all background tasks without requiring a task manager or a queue.

The second hazard is silent exception loss. When a fire-and-forget task raises an unhandled exception, Python does not print a traceback by default. The exception is attached to the task object and discarded when the task is garbage-collected. In a research loop tick that spawns background enrichment tasks and then moves on, a failed enrichment will fail silently unless something explicitly checks the task's result.

The fix is a done callback that inspects the exception. Register the callback with add_done_callback. Inside the callback, check whether the task was cancelled and whether it carries an exception. If it does, log the exception at warning level. This callback runs on the event loop, not in a thread, and should never raise. The pattern is: check cancelled, check exception, log, return. The parent tick finishes on time. The enrichment may fail. But the failure is visible in the logs rather than lost.

In the interview, when background tasks in async systems come up, name both hazards. GC cancellation via weak references and silent exception loss. The fixes are one line each — a strong-ref set with done-callback discard, and a done-callback that logs exceptions without re-raising. Both are easy to miss and both cause hard-to-debug production failures.

chapters.title: Semantic Exception Classes
chapters.script:
When you write retry logic for a multi-source API client, you face a design decision: match on HTTP status codes inside each retry loop, or raise typed exceptions from the inner request function and match on exception types in the outer loop.

Status-code matching at every retry site means every call site must parse the same headers and codes. When an API changes its error format, every loop needs updating. Typed exceptions are a better model.

The inner request function — the one that actually makes the HTTP call — raises a typed exception for each failure category. A rate-limit exception carries the reset_at timestamp as a constructor argument. A not-found exception carries no payload. The retry loop then handles each type in its own branch: rate limit means sleep until reset then retry, not-found means re-raise immediately with no retries, unknown error means log and backoff. The inner function is the only place that knows about HTTP headers and status codes. Everything above it works with exception types.

The data-bearing constructor is the key detail. The retry loop does not need to re-parse response headers to calculate the sleep duration. The exception carries the already-parsed reset timestamp. This follows the same principle as Pydantic validation feedback injection: structured information from the failure site travels up the call stack as a first-class value, not as a string to re-parse at a second location.

In the interview, if API client design or retry architecture comes up, name this pattern as semantic exception classes. Typed exceptions replace status-code matching at every call site. Data-bearing constructors eliminate repeated header parsing. Non-retryable categories re-raise immediately rather than exhausting the retry budget.

chapters.title: Event-Loop Isolation for Incompatible Libraries
chapters.script:
Some libraries cannot run inside an already-running async event loop. They hang, raise errors about a running loop, or silently produce wrong results. The issue is that they assume they own the event loop they are called from. Calling them from inside LangGraph's event loop — which is already running — causes a hang or a RuntimeError.

The fix is thread delegation with event-loop isolation. Acquire the coarse-grained concurrency lock in the parent event loop, then hand the actual library call off to asyncio.to_thread. Inside the thread function, create a fresh event loop with asyncio.run and run the library code there. The library sees an event loop it owns. The parent event loop sees a thread future it can await. The two never share an event loop.

The concurrency lock belongs in the parent event loop, not inside the thread. If you put the lock inside the thread, you need either a threading semaphore — a different primitive — or an asyncio semaphore created inside the thread's fresh loop, which cannot be shared with other callers. Acquiring the asyncio semaphore before the to_thread call bounds total concurrency across all callers while keeping the lock in the shared context.

Timeout composition completes the pattern. The parent await carries a total time budget. Inside the thread, a separate timeout primitive sets a hard cap on the library operation. If the inner timeout fires, the thread function catches it, kills any lingering child processes from the library, and returns an error dict. The parent's to_thread await surfaces a TimeoutError separately if the thread itself hangs past the outer budget. Two independent timeouts, two independent cancellation paths, no shared state between them.

In the interview, if integrating third-party libraries with incompatible async assumptions comes up, name the four elements: coarse-grained lock in the parent event loop, asyncio.to_thread for delegation, fresh asyncio.run inside the thread, and nested timeouts for each cancellation level.

chapters.title: Nested Timeout Layers
chapters.script:
A graph node that calls an external service can hang if the service never responds. The simplest fix is a timeout on the HTTP client. But HTTP timeouts are not the only way a graph can hang: a retry loop that keeps retrying, a streaming response that never closes, a checkpoint write blocked on a busy connection — these all bypass HTTP-level timeouts.

The production pattern is nested timeout layers with different roles. The inner timeout is a soft deadline passed through the graph state as a regular field. Every node that runs a network call reads the remaining deadline and applies it as its local time budget. The outer timeout is a hard ceiling on the entire ainvoke call, set above the soft deadline by a grace margin — typically sixty seconds. The soft deadline is what the graph tries to cooperatively respect. The hard ceiling is what asyncio enforces if the graph fails to respect it.

The difference matters when something misbehaves. If a node ignores its deadline, the outer asyncio.wait_for fires and raises a TimeoutError. That exception propagates out of ainvoke, is caught by the caller, and marks the run as failed with the exception type and message. A silent hang — where the cron tick just never returns — becomes a diagnosed failure with a stacktrace.

For a five-minute cron loop, the inner deadline is 540 seconds and the outer ceiling is 600. The 60-second margin gives the graph room to complete a final node after the deadline signal fires, write the checkpoint, and exit cleanly. If the graph is still running at 600 seconds, something is genuinely stuck and the hard ceiling kills it.

In the interview, if cron-scheduled LLM workloads come up, describe nested timeout layers: a soft policy deadline threaded through graph state, and a hard asyncio ceiling set above it. The soft deadline is cooperative. The hard ceiling is a guarantee. Without the hard ceiling, one stuck call can hold a cron slot indefinitely.

chapters.title: Polite-Pool Participation and Request Tagging
chapters.script:
Some public research APIs operate tiered rate limits based on whether the client identifies itself. OpenAlex assigns identified clients to a polite pool that receives higher throughput than anonymous requests. The identification is a single query parameter — mailto, set to a contact email for the operator. Without it, the client shares quota with scrapers and automated crawlers. With it, the client gets a separate allowance and the API operator can reach out if your traffic looks unusual.

This is a one-line change with a meaningful throughput impact. It belongs in the client configuration, not scattered across call sites. Set the mailto from an environment variable with a sensible default, and include it in every request automatically. The API operator sees a consistent identifier across all your calls. You exit the shared-scraper quota pool without any authentication overhead.

Per-request semantic tagging is the observability complement. When the same HTTP retry wrapper handles multiple endpoints on the same API, log messages like "rate limited" or "retry attempt 2" are ambiguous without context. Including an api_name parameter in the retry wrapper — a short string like openalex.author_profiles or openalex.citing_works — makes every log line from the retry machinery identify which call class is throttling, retrying, or failing. When you have six different OpenAlex call patterns in a single enrichment graph, that tag is the difference between diagnosing a problem in two minutes and spending an hour correlating log timestamps.

In the interview, if external API integration comes up, name these two practices together. Polite-pool registration via client identification reduces shared-quota contention. Per-request semantic tagging surfaces which endpoint is misbehaving in the logs. Both are trivial to implement and both produce disproportionate operational value.

chapters.title: Identity-Provenance Deduplication
chapters.script:
Standard deduplication matches records by a single key — an email address, a full name, a username. This works until two different real people share that key. A name-based dedup that merges two researchers with similar names does not produce a duplicate-free dataset. It produces a corrupted one, with one person's professional profile silently overwritten by another's.
